title: The mountain that needed mercury
learnerQuestion: Why did a silver mountain in the Andes come to depend on a mercury mine hundreds of kilometres away?
sensitiveContentNotice: This Story discusses conscripted labour and mercury poisoning.

header.whereLine: Villa Imperial de Potosí · Audiencia de Charcas · Viceroyalty of Peru

paragraphs.text: Here is the thing about a silver mountain: from the early 1570s, an increasingly important way of getting silver out of this one required mercury.
Before then, Andean smelters refined Cerro Rico's ore in wind-driven furnaces called *huayras*, and smelting continued alongside amalgamation afterwards.
What Potosí's refiners adopted in the early 1570s was mercury amalgamation, which lost mercury as it went: some was recovered, but refining at scale needed a continuing supply of replacement mercury.
The mercury came from another mine, and the crown decided who at Potosí received it.
That dependency — a silver mountain that needed a mercury mine — is the Story.
In 1573 this is the Villa Imperial de Potosí, within the Audiencia de Charcas — the jurisdiction seated at Ciudad de La Plata — within the Viceroyalty of Peru, governed from Ciudad de los Reyes.
These settlement and jurisdiction names were used in this period; present-day orientation is a toggle above the map, not a substitute for them.
The viceroy is Francisco de Toledo, in office since 1569.
The two seats are on the map because the jurisdictions are. Their boundaries are not drawn, because they have not been researched.
Here is where it gets interesting.
Amalgamation refines silver ore with mercury. Some mercury was recovered, but losses during processing meant that refining at scale needed a continuing supply of replacement mercury.
So the question "how did Potosí refine its silver?" turns into "where did Potosí's mercury come from?" — and the answer is a Place on this map that is not Potosí.
Two things complicate the tidy version.
The first is who did the work. From 1573 the *mita*, a rotational labour draft, conscripted workers for Potosí from sixteen highland provinces of the Viceroyalty of Peru.
Accounts from the colonial period describe workers at Huancavelica and in the Potosí refineries suffering mercury poisoning.
This Story tells the refining change and the harm together.
The second is whose account this pilot draws on. The administrative and technical accounts selected for this pilot were written by Spanish colonial authors, including refinery owners and clergy.

The one Andean-authored account in this pilot's evidence is Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala's *El primer nueva corónica y buen gobierno*, written around 1615 — roughly forty years after 1573 — and containing a sustained critique of colonial labour, including the *mita*.
It is one voice, writing later, in a petitionary mode.
This pilot has not yet identified testimony from conscripted workers about the work or about the poisoning; no additional record was identified in this documented search.

What changed, then? Historians generally explain the sharp rise in Potosí's registered silver output after the mid-1570s as the combined effect of four things: amalgamation refining, a viceregal mercury supply, the reorganised *mita* labour draft, and new water-powered mills along the Ribera.
This Story has followed the first two, and named the third: the people conscripted to work it.

The fourth has not been researched here. One of the four depended on a source far beyond Potosí: mercury from Huancavelica, administered under the crown's monopoly — and that is the Connection this Story exists to show.
It is the mainstream explanation, and it is an interpretation; the Claim beneath this paragraph says whose it is and what it rests on.

**Not yet researched.** This pilot holds one Story and one Connection. The paths that would lead out of here — what came before, what followed, what was happening elsewhere at the same time — have not been researched, so none is offered. The other Places on the map are in view to locate this Story, not to begin another. When a path is researched, it will appear here with its own Claims and Evidence.

profile.statusLine: Draft · not yet editorially reviewed. The counts below come from our working records; no historian has checked them yet. Rules version 0.1, draft.

warnings.name: Evidence concentrated in colonial Sources
warnings.text: Of the four primary documents behind this Story, three are by Spanish colonial authors (`C10`); the one Andean-authored account is cited as context or as the subject of a Claim, never as support (`C13`). 24 of 26 supporting citations descend, as recorded, from Spanish colonial authors or colonial administrative records. This tells you whose side of events the evidence comes from. It does not weigh the Story's conclusions.

warnings.name: Some voices missing
warnings.text: Testimony from conscripted workers about the work or the poisoning: not identified in this documented search (`C10`, `C13`). Three voices are listed below.

independence.byClaimSentence: 7 of the 12 Claims rest on a single group; 1 on two; 1 on three; for 1 we cannot tell (C09); 2 have no supporting Evidence yet (C11, C12). Twenty-six citations are not twenty-six confirmations. And independent does not mean reliable: this check counts how many Sources stand on their own, not how good any one of them is.
